messages.author: 68c425efdf6bd7f6
messages.subject: Interpretation of random walk coefficients
parts:
Dear all,

I would like to know how the regression coefficients of a random walk prior (rw2) are to be interpreted. Please see the graph attached. Does the spike in the graph e.g. mean that persons aged around 17 have a risk of 1.2 as compared to all other age groups?

I am just wondering as such an interpretation would pretty much mean that all persons aged 17 or older have a higher risk, which in this case does not make any real sense for persons aged 80 and older (I would expect a lower risk for this age group).

What is the correct way to communicate these regression coefficients?

Many thanks in advance.

Best,

Boris

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpretation of random walk coefficients
parts:
Hi,

is the rw2 process and an intercept the only model components? Model
component interpretation usually depends on what other model
components were included,
so it's hard to provide a clear answer without more details of what
the model looks like, and what the odds ratio is calculated with
respect to.

Finn.

messages.author: 68c425efdf6bd7f6
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpretation of random walk coefficients
parts:
Hi Finn,

The model is a Poisson model (number of GP visits per person), a and b are variables at the individual level (coded as 0 and 1), c and d are variables at the aggregated level (e.g. GPs per 100.000 persons). Additionally, I used a besag prior to account for spatial proximity.

this is the code I used.


model <- inla(GP_contacts~  1 + a+ b+ c+ d+
                           f(idx.alter, AGE, model = "rw2", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))) + 
                             f(idx1, model = "besag",
                               graph = "D:/INLA/Gyn", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.001)))), 
                           family = "poisson", data=Gesamt, control.compute = list(dic=T, openmp.strategy = "huge"),
                           control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb", reordering = "amdc"), verbose = T)

summary(model)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpretation of random walk coefficients
parts:
OK,
then the rw2 component can be (mostly) interpreted as the age effect
that is not explained by the combination of the other components. If
any of the other components, such as a,b,c, and d also vary with age,
then the rw2 component by itself doesn't give the absolute relative
risk per age. The peak at 17 therefore needs to be set in relation to
what the rest of the model says. For example, it might be picking up
some nonlinear effect that the linear covariate models can't
represent.
But perhaps more importantly, you really need to include the posterior
uncertainty when plotting the results before drawing too strong
conclusions.

Finn

Thank you very much for your answer, Finn.

I do understand that the coefficients are to be interpreted in relation to what the rest of the model says. However, I would like to know what the precise communication of the results of the rw2 model then is.

Is the precise wording e.g. "persons aged 17 years have a 1.22 higher risk than all other age groups after accounting for a,b,c and d"

Also, the uncertainty is plotted in the graph - thanks for the hint. However, as this is a dataset with 800.000 individuals, the uncertainty is quite small.

Many thanks in advance, Boris

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpretation of random walk coefficients
parts:
On Wed, 22 May 2019 at 12:52, 'Boris' via R-inla discussion group
<r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> I do understand that the coefficients are to be interpreted in relation to what the rest of the model says. However, I would like to know what the precise communication of the results of the rw2 model then is.
>
> Is the precise wording e.g. "persons aged 17 years have a 1.22 higher risk than all other age groups after accounting for a,b,c and d"

No, that can't be right, since all age groups above 10 have odds ratio
above 1; the 17 year olds just have higher than the others, not 1.22
higher! E.g., for age group 20 it's close to 1.2, so nearly the same
as for 17.
The graph label says "odds ratio", but you're talking about the rw2
component; I'm not sure how you get the former from the latter. You
may need to be more specific in how you define that odds ratio, so
that there is no doubt about what the risk is elevated in relation
_to_; unfortunately I haven't worked with that kind of model, so can't
give very specific advice on that point.
I suspect that "persons aged 17 years have a 22% higher risk than
explained by the covariates alone" (or "the rest of the model") is a
valid statement, but to compare the age groups with each other, I
suspect you need to do that more explicitly.
> Also, the uncertainty is plotted in the graph - thanks for the hint. However, as this is a dataset with 800.000 individuals, the uncertainty is quite small.

Ahhh, yes, I see the tiny grey bands now!

Finn
